articles.title: SpaceX-Tesla merger: How to tackle China risk
articles.summary: Elon Musk's potential mega-merger of Tesla and SpaceX would likely face a China-shaped hurdle from regulators on both sides of the Pacific over concerns about national security and the sharing of data and technology.The world's richest person said on Tuesday his two companies had set up special committees to discuss a union, calling a merger a "good idea". Turning it into reality, however, would mean navigating the thorny issue of Tesla's heavy reliance on China for manufacturing versus SpaceX's defence business.Rocket company SpaceX is increasingly reliant on sensitive US government and defence contracts, which could subject any merger involving Tesla's business in China to intense scrutiny on national security grounds.Also read: What to know about the Ebola outbreak that has spread from Congo to 4 other countriesChinese regulators also require Tesla to keep confidential user data collected by its automated driving systems firmly in China, and any firewall would have to prevent the flow of information or technology in either direction.Below are some ways that Musk and the companies could look to clear any barriers put up by Washington or Beijing.Could Tesla keep its China business?One potential option would be for the merged company to create a firewall around Tesla's Chinese operations to block access to sensitive data from SpaceX and other parts of the business. Such a move is not unheard of, said Daniel Kollar, head of automotive and mobility practice at consultancy Intralink Group.Plenty of companies have been able to run major defence businesses outside of China while maintaining operations in the country, he said, citing Airbus and Honeywell.Also read: Beyond the ballot: Why Israel's next leader may stick to Netanyahu's doctrineSpaceX's defence-related businesses include Starshield, which develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.A two-way firewall would also likely be the minimum requirement to ensure Tesla's data from Chinese drivers stays in China, analysts said. Since 2021, Tesla has been complying with Beijing's requirement to keep all driver data inside of China.Tesla could continue to operate in China for years to come as a self-contained unit with its own research and development and strict agreements to keep all data inside China, said Michael Dunne, CEO of automotive advisory firm Dunne Insights, which closely follows China's auto industry.Keeping both Beijing and Washington happy about such a firewall, however, could be tricky, said Christopher Tang, a professor at UCLA's Anderson School of Management who specializes in ​global supply chains. He said the Chinese government is likely to try to use any proposed merger to negotiate a range of items as a condition for approval."China will use it as leverage," Tang said. "They have the bargaining power right now."Ioannis Kokkoris, professor of competition law and economics at Queen Mary University of London, identified two possible concessions that China could seek: access for Chinese companies to strategically significant technologies, and commitments to retain manufacturing capacity and investment in China.Any demand to share sensitive SpaceX-related technology, however, would run directly into US security restrictions.What about divestment?Analysts have said there were likely three broad paths towards divestment: a spinoff in which Tesla retains a majority economic interest, a sale paired with long-term brand licensing agreements, or an outright sale, possibly to another automaker.Any kind of divestment would come with plenty of complications, including the looming question of who would buy the asset. China's automakers, which do not need any extra capacity, are unlikely to be interested, said Li Yanwei, an analyst at the China Automobile Dealers Association.Many foreign automakers, on the other hand, are already strapped for cash, making them unlikely buyers as well. Kollar said Musk would be more likely to sell the China operation off for parts rather than hand control to anyone else.But Kollar added that unless Musk wanted to signal a retreat from the auto business, he expected Tesla to find a way to retain its China operations under the existing ownership structure.Tesla China and China's State Administration of Market Regulation did not reply to requests for comment.China still needed for cash flowA clean break from China could be difficult. Chinese suppliers are deeply integrated in Musk's broader empire and Tesla's Shanghai production accounted for more than 50% of its global output, according to Yale Zhang, managing director at Shanghai-based consultancy AutoForesight.Some investors, though, say those considerations aren't big enough to get in the way of a deal.Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, a Tesla and SpaceX investor, said Tesla's China manufacturing base is considerable, but the electric vehicle maker has already been making moves to expand US production, particularly for humanoid robots and the Cybercab driverless car, and many investors are more focused on Musk's promises for where these are headed.Mulberry also said he thinks Tesla would argue to US regulators that its China operations wouldn't overlap with SpaceX, but if unsuccessful, he thinks Tesla could shut or scale back its China production."It's short-term enough and small enough to be digestible," he said.Tang, the UCLA professor, said that while Tesla's future prospects may lie outside of China, its current EV business is heavily reliant on it. Much of the cash needed to finance its future bets comes from China EV production, he said."That is exactly why China will take advantage of this moment," Tang said. "Because you still need them."

Organised by the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI) with the approval of the International Kabaddi Federation (IKF), the championship will feature 23 squads and more than 400 athletes competing in 62 matches.
The championship was formally unveiled at a curtain-raiser event on Wednesday.
The Indian men's team will be captained by Surjeet Singh, while Nidhi Sharma will lead the women's team.
The participating nations are India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Canada, Singapore, Malaysia, Uganda, England, Scotland, and Australia.
The semifinals in both categories will take place on October 30, followed by the finals on October 31.
"It is a proud moment for Indian kabaddi to host the first Commonwealth Championship in Ahmedabad," said AKFI secretary Jitendra Pran Singh Thakur in a statement.

articles.title: How the Mecca defense agreement works
articles.summary: Ankara: Turkey's government has asked parliament to ratify a mutual defense agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, bringing the country closer to bolstering Saudi defenses as it faces attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels.Mirroring NATO's Article 5, the so-called Mecca Joint Defense Agreement commits the sides to view an armed attack against one as an attack on all three.While Turkey says that it's considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, officials have cautioned that the pact is defensive in nature and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.Turkish and Pakistani officials have also insisted that the pact isn't against Iran or any other country, but haven't said how they would react if attacked by Iran.Regional countries take responsibility for their securityThe agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Mecca in August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif with the aim of increasing cooperation and deterrence among the three regional heavyweights at a time of increased uncertainty amid the Iran war.It brings together oil-rich Saudi Arabia and nuclear power Pakistan as well as Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defense industry. It enables the three to take greater charge for their own security at a time of reduced U.S. involvement.For Pakistan, the Mecca Agreement builds on existing military ties with Riyadh. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate mutual defense agreement in September 2025.Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has repeatedly said that the Mecca agreement doesn't replace existing agreements and is open to other countries willing to uphold its principles and resolve differences peacefully.Nature of assistance planned is still unknownDuring an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. They didn't elaborate.Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Turkey and Pakistan were assessing possible air defense, electronic warfare and technical assistance for Saudi Arabia."What type of assistance can be provided, especially in areas such as air defense and electronic warfare, what technical support can be offered? Work on these issues is ongoing," he said."Turkey will not be sending troops into another country's territory to carry out an attack. It is a defense agreement," Fidan said, addressing concerns raised by opposition parties that Turkey would be drawn into the conflict in Yemen.Authorities in Pakistan have declined to disclose deployment details, citing operational confidentiality. Officials say, however, that Pakistan's role would be strictly defensive. The Pakistani Information Ministry recently dismissed as "speculative" news reports that said Pakistan had already deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia.Comment from Saudi Arabia on the pact since the Houthi attacks has been limited. In a post on X following a visit by Pakistan's army chief, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman said: "We affirmed our commitment to continuing joint efforts to confront these attacks in accordance with the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense."10-year commitment to the pactLittle was known about the content of the pact until Turkey's government submitted it to parliament for approval on Tuesday.The 16-article agreement, published by Turkish state broadcaster TRT on its website, states that the countries would defend each other militarily in case of external aggression in line with the U.N. Charter's right of self-defense.The agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, including joint training programs, exercises and personnel exchanges. It allows cooperation in the defense industry, including joint weapons production and technology transfers as well as intelligence sharing.A surprise clause states that the parties wouldn't be able to withdraw from the pact for 10 years, after which they would need to provide a three-month notice to leave.A parliamentary committee is expected to review the agreement in the coming days before it reaches the Turkish parliament's general assembly for ratification. Separately, Turkey's parliament would have to authorize any deployment of Turkish military personnel.Pakistan's potential contributionsPakistan hasn't sought parliamentary endorsement of the Mecca agreement, but officials say the government and other national institutions support it. They say Islamabad would provide whatever military assistance Saudi Arabia needs to defend the kingdom and Islam's holiest sites.Pakistan's military has more than two decades of experience fighting militant groups, which analysts say could help it bolster Saudi defenses.The agreement builds on decades of Pakistani military service in Saudi Arabia. An unspecified number of Pakistani troops have been stationed in Saudi Arabia since the early 1980s to train and advise Saudi forces.Pact to be led by retired Pakistani generalEven before the ratification process has been completed, the three countries established and convened a meeting of the so-called Strategic Political and Defense Committee composed of the foreign ministers, defense ministers and chiefs of staff.The committee is expected to meet twice a year.The pact's secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will serve a three-year term.

articles.title: Essar Ports wins ₹2,276 crore Tuna Tekra terminal project at Kandla
articles.summary:
Essar Ports has secured a letter of award from Deendayal Port Authority to develop an 18.33-million-tonne-a-year multipurpose cargo terminal at Tuna Tekra in Gujarat's Kandla port, marking a renewed push by the group to expand its ports business.
The project carries an estimated cost of Rs 2,276.06 crore, including an investment of Rs 1,552.57 crore by Essar Ports and Rs 723.49 crore by the port authority, the company said in a statement.
The terminal will be developed under a 30-year build-operate-transfer concession through the public-private partnership route, with Essar emerging as the highest bidder in a global competitive bidding process.
The project will add capacity for handling dry and other multipurpose cargo on India's western coast, as the country seeks to expand port infrastructure to accommodate growing trade and improve logistics efficiency, it said.
The proposed facility will have four berths, each measuring 300 metres, providing a total berth length of 1,200 metres

articles.title: India must make growth employment-intensive, not just fast: Ex-RBI chief
articles.summary:
Sustaining economic growth of 7 per cent or more will require stronger private investment, labour-intensive manufacturing, better human capital and deeper integration into global value chains, former RBI Governor D Subbarao has said.
Subbarao also said that the challenge is not merely to grow fast, but to make growth productive, employment-intensive and resilient.
"India's 7.8 per cent growth in the first quarter suggests that the economy is more resilient than many expected...I am optimistic about India's medium-term prospects, but not complacent," he told PTI.
